# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**ARIES physiological logging.** The ARIES protocol (Mohan et al., 1992) is the canonical WAL design. Every update generates a log record identified by a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number (LSN)**; each page carries a **pageLSN** recording the LSN of the last update applied to it. The WAL rule requires that a log record be forced to stable storage before the dirty page it describes is written (steal policy) and before commit is acknowledged (no-force policy). ARIES uses *physiological* records: physical addressing to a page, logical description of the intra-page change, which allows redo to be page-idempotent while undo tolerates intervening page reorganization. **Compensation Log Records (CLRs)** log undo actions themselves; a CLR's **undoNextLSN** pointer makes rollback restartable without re-undoing work, bounding log growth during repeated crashes. The in-memory **Transaction Table** (lastLSN, status per transaction) and **Dirty Page Table** (recLSN = earliest LSN that may not be reflected on disk) are checkpointed to bound recovery work.

**Group commit.** Forcing the log at every commit makes fsync latency the throughput ceiling. Group commit batches multiple transactions' commit records into a single log flush: a committing transaction waits briefly so that one `fsync`/`fdatasync` amortizes across many commits. MySQL/InnoDB implements a three-stage group commit coordinated with the binary log (binlog) via an internal 2PC between the engine redo log and binlog; PostgreSQL exposes `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings`. Modern variants pipeline WAL writes using per-insertion locks and reserved byte ranges (PostgreSQL's WAL insertion slots) so copying into the log buffer is parallel while flush order is preserved.

**Torn-page protection: full-page writes and the doublewrite buffer.** A crash mid-way through writing an 8–16 KB page over 512 B/4 KB sectors yields a *torn page* that physiological redo cannot repair (redo assumes the page is internally consistent). PostgreSQL's **full_page_writes** logs the entire page image on the first modification after each checkpoint, so redo can restore the page wholesale. InnoDB instead uses the **doublewrite buffer**: pages are first written sequentially to a dedicated doublewrite area, fsync'd, then written in place; after a crash, any torn page is recovered from the doublewrite copy (validated via page checksums). The trade-off is WAL volume (PostgreSQL) versus doubled page-write bandwidth (InnoDB), both mitigated on atomic-write-capable storage.

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**PostgreSQL append-only tuple versioning.** Each heap tuple carries **xmin** (creating transaction ID) and **xmax** (deleting/updating XID). An update creates a new tuple version in place in the heap; the old version's xmax is set, and chains are linked via **ctid**. A **snapshot** (xmin horizon, xmax, in-progress XID list) plus the commit-status log (**pg_xact/CLOG**) and **hint bits** determine visibility. Because dead versions accumulate in the heap, **VACUUM** must reclaim them, freeze old XIDs to prevent **transaction-ID wraparound**, and maintain the visibility map enabling index-only scans. **HOT (Heap-Only Tuples)** avoids index churn when updated columns aren't indexed.

**Undo-based versioning (Oracle, InnoDB).** Rather than versioning in place, Oracle and InnoDB update pages *in place* and store before-images in **rollback segments / undo logs**. A reader with an older **read view** (InnoDB's term: low/high water marks over trx IDs) follows the **DB_ROLL_PTR** in each clustered-index record back through the undo chain to reconstruct the version visible to its snapshot. Garbage collection is the **purge** of undo once no read view needs it; long-running queries cause Oracle's classic `ORA-01555 snapshot too old`. The structural contrast with PostgreSQL: reads of old data pay reconstruction cost, but the primary storage stays compact without vacuum.

**Snapshot Isolation and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain SI (first-committer-wins on write-write conflicts) is not serializable: it permits **write skew** (two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint items, violating an invariant) and the batch/read-only anomaly. Cahill, Röhm, and Fekete's **SSI**, productionized in PostgreSQL 9.1's SERIALIZABLE level, tracks **rw-antidependencies** via SIREAD predicate locks: a cycle in the serialization graph under SI must contain two consecutive rw-antidependency edges (a "dangerous structure") with the pivot transaction; detecting that structure and aborting one participant guarantees serializability, at the cost of false-positive aborts.

## 3. LSM Trees

**Memtable → SSTable flush pipeline.** Writes land in a WAL and an in-memory **memtable** (typically a skip list in RocksDB/LevelDB). When full, the memtable becomes immutable and is flushed as a **Sorted String Table (SSTable)** — an immutable, sorted, block-compressed run with a block index and footer. This converts random writes into sequential I/O, the core LSM proposition from O'Neil et al.'s original LSM-tree paper.

**Compaction policies: leveled vs. size-tiered.** **Leveled compaction** (LevelDB/RocksDB default beyond L0) maintains levels of exponentially increasing capacity (~10×) where each level ≥ L1 contains non-overlapping key ranges; compaction merges one SSTable into the overlapping files of the next level. It minimizes **space amplification** (~1.1×) and read amplification but maximizes **write amplification** (often 10–30×). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS, Cassandra)** merges similarly sized runs within a tier: low write amplification, but high space amplification (duplicate versions across overlapping runs) and worse reads. RocksDB's **universal compaction** and hybrid schemes (Lazy Leveling in the Dostoevsky paper) navigate this continuum — a concrete instance of the **RUM conjecture** (you can't simultaneously optimize Read, Update, and Memory/space overheads).

**Read-path optimizations: Bloom filters and fence pointers.** A point lookup must consult the memtable, every L0 file, and one file per deeper level. Per-SSTable **Bloom filters** (typically ~10 bits/key for ~1% false positives) skip runs that cannot contain the key; **fence pointers** (per-block index entries) locate the single block to read within a chosen SSTable. **Monkey** (Dasgupta et al.) showed optimal filter-memory allocation skews bits toward smaller levels. Range scans cannot use Bloom filters (prefix Bloom filters partially help), which is why compaction aggressiveness matters for scan-heavy workloads. Deletes are **tombstones** that must survive compaction until they reach the bottommost level.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Splits, merges, and rebalancing.** An insert into a full leaf triggers a **node split**: half the keys move to a new right sibling and a **separator key** is posted to the parent, possibly cascading to a root split (the only way the tree grows in height, preserving perfect balance). Deletions that drop a node below the fill threshold trigger **merging (coalescing)** with a sibling or **key redistribution (rotation)**; many production engines (e.g., InnoDB) merge lazily or only on emptiness since workloads rarely shrink monotonically. These **structure modification operations (SMOs)** must appear atomic to concurrent operations and be logged so recovery never observes a half-split tree (ARIES uses nested top actions / dummy CLRs so completed SMOs are not undone by transaction rollback).

**Latch crabbing and Blink-trees.** Traversal uses **latch coupling (crabbing)**: acquire the child's latch before releasing the parent's, releasing ancestors once the child is "safe" (won't split/merge). Pessimistic crabbing with exclusive latches on the whole path kills concurrency, so engines use optimistic descent with read latches and restart on conflict. The **Blink-tree** (Lehman & Yao) is the elegant alternative: every node carries a **right-sibling link** and a **high key**; a split first creates the right sibling and link, then posts the separator upward as a separate step. A concurrent reader that lands on a just-split node detects (via the high key) that its target moved right and simply chases the link — allowing lock-free-ish descent with at most a few latches held. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Blink-tree.

**Key-range (next-key) locking.** Serializability over a B+tree requires **phantom protection**: locking logical key ranges, not just existing keys. **ARIES/KVL (Key-Value Locking)** and **ARIES/IM (Index Management)** lock the gap by locking the *next key*: an insert into a gap must acquire a lock on the following key (instant IX in KVL) to detect conflicting range scans. InnoDB's implementation is **next-key locking** (record lock + preceding **gap lock**) at REPEATABLE READ and above. Crucially, latches (physical, short-duration, deadlock-avoided by ordering) are distinct from locks (logical, transaction-duration, deadlock-detected) — conflating them is a classic design error.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**The base protocol with presumed-abort/presumed-commit.** The coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant force-writes a *prepared* log record (making it **in-doubt** — it can no longer unilaterally abort) and votes; on unanimous YES the coordinator force-writes *commit* and broadcasts the decision; participants force a commit record and ACK. **Presumed abort (PrA)** — the de facto standard, used in the XA model — lets the coordinator forget aborted transactions immediately: if a recovering participant inquires and the coordinator has no record, the answer is abort. This eliminates the abort force-write and ACKs for aborts, and lets read-only participants vote READ-ONLY and drop out after phase one. **Presumed commit (PrC)** inverts the presumption, saving messages for the common commit case but requiring the coordinator to force-log the participant set *before* prepare.

**The blocking problem.** 2PC is a blocking protocol: if the coordinator fails after participants prepare but before they learn the outcome, those participants are **in-doubt** and must hold all locks (including, under 2PL, read locks) indefinitely — they cannot abort (coordinator may have committed) nor commit (another participant may have voted NO). Timeouts help only before the prepare point; the **cooperative termination protocol** (asking peer participants) resolves in-doubt state only if some peer knows the decision. This is the precise sense in which atomic commit with a single coordinator cannot be non-blocking under crash failures — consistent with the FLP-adjacent impossibility results for commit protocols.

**Non-blocking enhancements: 3PC and consensus-replicated coordination.** **Three-phase commit (Skeen)** inserts a *pre-commit* phase so that no participant commits while another could still be unaware of an impending commit, achieving non-blocking termination under crash-stop failures with a synchronous network — but it is unsafe under network partitions, which is why it's rarely deployed. The practical fix is **Paxos Commit** (Gray & Lamport): make the commit *decision itself* a consensus instance (or run one Paxos instance per participant vote), removing the coordinator as a single point of failure. **Google Spanner** operationalizes this by layering 2PC over Paxos groups: each participant and the coordinator are themselves Paxos-replicated state machines, so coordinator "failure" is just a leader failover and in-doubt windows shrink to leader-election time. Calvin-style deterministic databases avoid 2PC's runtime voting altogether by pre-ordering transactions.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport clocks.** Lamport (1978) defined the **happened-before relation (→)**: a partial order induced by program order and message send/receive. A **Lamport clock** is a scalar counter: increment on each local event; on receive, set `C = max(C_local, C_msg) + 1`. This guarantees the **clock condition** (a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b)), and with process-ID tiebreaking yields a total order usable for distributed mutual exclusion and deterministic replicated state machines. The converse does not hold: C(a) < C(b) does *not* imply causality — Lamport clocks cannot *detect* concurrency.

**Vector clocks and version vectors.** A **vector clock** assigns each of N processes a vector; entry *i* counts events at process *i*. Compare componentwise: VC(a) < VC(b) iff a → b; incomparable vectors mean the events are **concurrent**. This characterizes causality exactly (Fidge/Mattern). **Version vectors** are the per-object specialization used in **Dynamo** and Riak to detect **conflicting siblings** on read: incomparable versions are returned to the client (or a CRDT/merge function) for **semantic reconciliation**. Practical issues: vector growth with actor churn (mitigated by **dotted version vectors**, pruning) motivated Dynamo's truncation heuristics.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) vs. TrueTime.** **HLC** (Kulkarni et al.) combines a physical-clock component with a logical component: timestamps stay close to wall-clock time (bounded drift from NTP time) while preserving the Lamport clock condition, fitting in 64 bits. **CockroachDB** uses HLC for MVCC timestamps and causality propagation across sessions; because HLC gives causal but not strict real-time ordering, Cockroach handles reads within a clock-offset **uncertainty interval** with read restarts. Contrast **Spanner's TrueTime**, which is *not* a logical clock: GPS/atomic-clock hardware exposes a bounded uncertainty interval [earliest, latest], and **commit-wait** (holding a commit until `latest` of its timestamp has passed) buys **external consistency (linearizability of transactions)** — physical-time guarantees that purely logical clocks cannot provide.

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Majority read/write quorums and Dynamo-style variants.** In an N-replica register, choosing read quorum R and write quorum W with **R + W > N** guarantees read-write intersection (every read sees the latest completed write's replicas), and **W + W > N** (W > N/2) prevents conflicting concurrent writes. Note the standard caveat: R+W>N alone gives *regular* semantics, not linearizability, without read-repair/write-back of the observed value (ABD algorithm). **Dynamo/Cassandra** make (N, R, W) tunable per operation; under failure they use **sloppy quorums** — writes go to the first N *healthy* nodes on the ring, not necessarily the home replicas — with **hinted handoff** delivering the write to the proper owner upon recovery. Sloppy quorums sacrifice the intersection guarantee (hence eventual consistency plus anti-entropy via **Merkle trees**) for availability.

**Consensus quorums: intersection in Paxos/Raft.** Paxos and Raft rely on the fact that any two **majority quorums intersect**: a value chosen by one majority is discovered by any later leader reading a majority (phase-1 / RequestVote with log-completeness check in Raft). Raft's election restriction — a candidate must have a log at least as up-to-date (last term, then length) as each voter's — plus the rule that a leader only counts entries from its own term as committed (the Figure 8 anomaly) are both consequences of quorum intersection reasoning. These quorums tolerate f failures with N = 2f+1.

**Flexible quorums and witnesses.** **Flexible Paxos (FPaxos, Howard et al.)** proved the real requirement is only that *phase-1 (leader election) quorums intersect phase-2 (replication) quorums* — not that phase-2 quorums intersect each other. So a 5-node group can commit with any 2 replicas (fast steady state) if elections require 4 — trading failover-time availability for commit latency. **Witness replicas** (vote-only nodes storing little or no data, as in Spanner's witness regions and CockroachDB non-voting/witness configurations) cheapen quorum formation across regions. Grid and tree quorum systems generalize further, trading **quorum size, load, and fault tolerance** per Naor–Wool's quorum-system theory.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-phase restart.** (a) **Analysis** scans from the last checkpoint, rebuilding the Transaction Table (loser transactions) and Dirty Page Table, computing the redo start point (min recLSN). (b) **Redo** *repeats history*: every logged update — including those of losers and even CLRs — is reapplied if `pageLSN < record LSN`, restoring the exact pre-crash state. Repeating history is the key ARIES insight: it makes undo correct even with fine-grained (record-level) locking and physiological logging. (c) **Undo** rolls back losers in reverse LSN order across all transactions simultaneously (following prevLSN chains), writing **CLRs** whose undoNextLSN ensures idempotent, never-undone-twice recovery across repeated crashes. ARIES supports steal/no-force buffering, partial rollbacks via **savepoints**, and **nested top actions** for non-undoable structure changes.

**Checkpointing disciplines.** A **sharp (consistent) checkpoint** quiesces updates and flushes all dirty pages — simple but creates latency cliffs. ARIES-style **fuzzy checkpoints** merely log snapshots of the DPT and transaction table without flushing, letting the background writer flush continuously; recovery cost is bounded by the oldest recLSN, so engines also track and advance the flush horizon (InnoDB's fuzzy checkpointing tied to redo-log capacity and its `log_sys` flushed_to_disk_lsn; PostgreSQL's spread checkpoints with `checkpoint_completion_target`). Correct checkpointing is what bounds the analysis/redo scan — without it, recovery time grows with total log volume.

**Shadow paging — the historical contrast.** **System R's** recovery used **shadow paging**: updates write new page copies; commit atomically swings the page-table root from shadow to current version, so recovery is nearly free (discard current, keep shadow). Costs that killed it for high-performance OLTP: destroyed physical clustering, page-granularity commits, expensive garbage collection, and poor concurrency — the precise motivations Mohan cites for ARIES. The idea survives in **copy-on-write B-trees** (LMDB's fully CoW design needs no WAL at all; Btrfs/ZFS at the filesystem layer) and in **SQLite's rollback journal vs. WAL mode** dichotomy, which recapitulates the undo-journal vs. redo-log design space. LSM engines, meanwhile, recover by replaying the WAL into a fresh memtable — immutable SSTables need no redo — showing how storage architecture dictates recovery architecture.

---

**Synthesis.** The through-line: every mechanism above is an answer to one of three questions — *how do we make effects durable and atomic* (WAL, CLRs, doublewrite, ARIES, shadow paging, 2PC/Paxos Commit), *how do we let concurrent actors proceed without observing broken intermediate states* (MVCC snapshots, SSI, latch crabbing, Blink-trees, next-key locking), and *how do we order and agree on events without shared memory or perfect clocks* (Lamport/vector/hybrid clocks, majority and flexible quorums). Production systems compose them: Spanner = 2PC + Paxos quorums + TrueTime + Paxos-group WAL; PostgreSQL = ARIES-style WAL + append-only MVCC + Blink-trees + SSI; RocksDB = WAL + memtable/LSM + Bloom filters, with recovery by log replay.

Answer: The brief above covers all eight areas with ≥3 precisely named mechanisms each — WAL (ARIES physiological logging/LSN/CLR, group commit, full-page writes & doublewrite buffer); MVCC (PostgreSQL xmin/xmax+VACUUM, InnoDB/Oracle undo-based read views, SI anomalies & SSI rw-antidependency detection); LSM trees (memtable→SSTable flush, leveled vs. size-tiered/universal compaction, Bloom filters & fence pointers); B+tree maintenance (splits/merges/SMOs with nested top actions, latch crabbing & Lehman-Yao Blink-trees, ARIES/KVL–ARIES/IM next-key/gap locking); 2PC (presumed abort/commit, the blocking problem & cooperative termination, 3PC and Paxos Commit/Spanner 2PC-over-Paxos); logical clocks (Lamport clocks, vector clocks/version vectors, HLC vs. TrueTime commit-wait); quorum systems (R+W>N majority quorums with sloppy quorums/hinted handoff, Paxos/Raft quorum intersection, Flexible Paxos & witness replicas); and crash recovery (ARIES analysis/redo/undo with repeating history, fuzzy vs. sharp checkpoints, shadow paging and its CoW descendants).

# Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and Crash Recovery: Technical Findings

## Part 1: Write-Ahead Logging

### The WAL Protocol (Fundamental Invariants)

Write-ahead logging enforces two rules:

1. **WAL rule (atomicity/undo rule):** A log record describing a change to a page must be durably written to stable storage *before* the modified (dirty) page is flushed to disk. This guarantees undo information is available if the page reaches disk before commit.
2. **Force-log-at-commit rule (durability/redo rule):** All log records for a transaction, up to and including its COMMIT record, must be forced to stable storage before the transaction is acknowledged as committed. This permits a **no-force** buffer policy (dirty pages need not be flushed at commit).

Together these enable the **steal/no-force** buffer management policy — the highest-performance quadrant — which is exactly what ARIES was designed to support: *steal* (uncommitted dirty pages may be written to disk, requiring undo) and *no-force* (committed pages need not be written at commit, requiring redo).

### Mechanism 1: ARIES-Style Physiological Logging

**ARIES** (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics; Mohan et al., IBM, 1992) uses **physiological logging**: log records are *physical to a page* (identify a specific page) but *logical within the page* (e.g., "insert tuple t into page P" rather than a byte-level diff). This is a compromise between pure physical logging (large records, but idempotent) and pure logical logging (compact, but hard to make redo-safe when operations span pages).

Key data structures:

- **LSN (Log Sequence Number):** A monotonically increasing identifier for each log record, typically the record's byte offset in the log file. LSNs totally order all logged updates.
- **pageLSN:** Each database page stores, in its header, the LSN of the most recent log record that modified it. During redo, a logged update is reapplied **only if pageLSN < record's LSN**, making physiological redo idempotent (this is the "LSN comparison" or "LSN gating" test).
- **prevLSN:** Each log record contains the LSN of the previous record written by the *same transaction*, forming a backward-linked chain per transaction used for undo/rollback.
- **Transaction Table (TT):** In-memory table of active transactions; for each, its state (running, committing, aborting) and **lastLSN** (most recent log record). Reconstructed during recovery's analysis pass.
- **Dirty Page Table (DPT):** In-memory table of pages that are dirty in the buffer pool; for each page, the **recLSN (recovery LSN)** — the LSN of the *first* log record that dirtied the page since it was last flushed. The minimum recLSN over the DPT bounds where redo must begin.
- **CLR (Compensation Log Record):** A redo-only log record written when an update is *undone* (during rollback or crash recovery). Each CLR carries an **undoNextLSN** pointer to the next log record of that transaction that still needs undoing, so that undo work is never repeated across repeated crashes. CLRs are **never undone**, which bounds undo work and guarantees recovery progress even with crashes during recovery (restart idempotence).

ARIES also supports **nested top actions** (e.g., structure modification operations in B-trees / index page splits) via dummy CLRs, so physical structure changes survive logically even if the enclosing transaction aborts, and **save points / partial rollback** via the prevLSN chain.

### Mechanism 2: Group Commit and Log Buffer Flushing

Log records are first appended to an in-memory **log buffer** (e.g., InnoDB's log buffer, PostgreSQL's WAL buffers). The force-at-commit rule requires an fsync (or equivalent, e.g., `fdatasync`, `O_DIRECT`+`O_DSYNC`) of the log at every commit — a latency-bound operation.

**Group commit** amortizes this cost: the system batches the commit records of multiple concurrently committing transactions into a *single* log flush/fsync. One transaction (the "leader") performs the flush up to the highest needed LSN; "follower" transactions whose commit LSN ≤ flushed LSN are released together. This converts N fsyncs into 1 per batch, dramatically raising commit throughput at a small latency cost.

Concrete implementations:
- **PostgreSQL:** `commit_delay` / `commit_siblings` tune deliberate batching; the WAL writer process and flush-up-to-LSN logic provide implicit group commit.
- **MySQL/InnoDB:** binary-log group commit (BLGC) with leader/follower stages (flush, sync, commit), coordinated with the InnoDB redo log via the two-phase commit between binlog and redo log; `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit` controls durability strictness (1 = flush+fsync per commit; 2 = flush per commit, fsync ~per second; 0 = both ~per second).
- Related relaxation: **asynchronous commit** (PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit = off`) acknowledges commit before the WAL flush, trading a bounded window of potential committed-transaction loss (but never corruption/inconsistency) for latency.

### Mechanism 3: Torn-Page Protection — Full-Page Writes and the Doublewrite Buffer

A **torn page** (partial page write) occurs when a crash interrupts a database page write that is larger than the storage device's atomic write unit (DB pages are typically 8 KB/16 KB vs. 512 B–4 KB sectors). The result is a page that is part-old, part-new. This breaks physiological redo: the pageLSN or intra-page structure may be inconsistent, so applying "logical within page" redo against a corrupt page is unsafe.

Two standard countermeasures:

- **PostgreSQL `full_page_writes` (FPW / full-page images):** The *first* time a page is modified after each checkpoint, PostgreSQL writes the entire page image (a **full-page image**, FPI) into the WAL rather than just the delta. During redo, the FPI physically overwrites the possibly-torn page, restoring a consistent base; subsequent physiological records then apply normally. Cost: WAL volume spikes after checkpoints (motivating longer checkpoint intervals and `wal_compression`).

- **MySQL InnoDB doublewrite buffer:** Before writing dirty pages to their final tablespace locations, InnoDB first writes them sequentially to a dedicated **doublewrite** area (historically in the system tablespace; separate doublewrite files since 8.0.20), fsyncs it, then writes pages to their home locations. On recovery, any torn page in the tablespace (detected via page checksum) is repaired from its intact copy in the doublewrite area. The redo log can then stay compact (physiological records only, no full-page images). Cost: roughly 2× page-write I/O volume, though the doublewrite portion is sequential.

- (Contrast/avoidance: copy-on-write/append-only storage engines — e.g., LMDB, or ZFS as a filesystem — never overwrite pages in place, so torn pages cannot occur; and on devices guaranteeing atomic writes of DB-page size, both mechanisms can be disabled.)

---

## Part 2: Crash Recovery

### Mechanism 1: ARIES Three-Phase Restart Recovery

On restart after a crash, ARIES runs three sequential passes over the log:

**Phase 1 — Analysis.** Start from the most recent **begin_checkpoint** record (located via the **master record** pointing to the last complete checkpoint) and scan *forward* to the end of the log. Reconstruct:
- the **Transaction Table**: which transactions were active at the crash (**losers**, to be undone) vs. committed/ended (**winners**);
- the **Dirty Page Table**: which pages *might* be dirty, each with its recLSN.
Output: the **redo start point** = min(recLSN) over the reconstructed DPT, and the set of loser transactions with their lastLSNs.

**Phase 2 — Redo ("repeating history").** Scan *forward* from min(recLSN), reapplying **every** logged update — including updates of loser transactions and previously logged CLRs — subject to two filters: (a) the page appears in the DPT with recLSN ≤ record's LSN, and (b) on reading the page, pageLSN < record's LSN. This **repeating history** principle is ARIES's signature design decision: it restores the database to its *exact* state at the instant of the crash before any undo occurs, which is what makes fine-granularity (record-level) locking, partial rollbacks, and logical undo correct.

**Phase 3 — Undo.** Roll back all loser transactions by processing their update records in *reverse LSN order* (a single backward sweep over the merged set of losers' lastLSN chains, following prevLSN / undoNextLSN pointers). For each update undone, write a **CLR** containing undoNextLSN. Because CLRs are redo-only and never undone, a crash *during* recovery never duplicates undo work — recovery is idempotent and makes guaranteed forward progress ("no undo of undo"). When a loser's chain is exhausted, write an **end** (abort-complete) record.

### Mechanism 2: Checkpointing — Fuzzy vs. Sharp

Checkpoints bound the length of the log that recovery must process.

- **Sharp (consistent) checkpoint:** Quiesce update activity (or at least halt new updates), flush **all** dirty pages to disk, and write a checkpoint record. After a sharp checkpoint, redo can start at the checkpoint — no DPT needed. Drawback: a massive, latency-spiking I/O burst and a pause in transaction processing; unacceptable for large buffer pools. (Sharp checkpoints survive in specific contexts, e.g., MySQL performs a sharp checkpoint at clean shutdown.)

- **Fuzzy checkpoint (ARIES-style):** No quiescing and no forced page flushing at checkpoint time. The system writes a **begin_checkpoint** record, then an **end_checkpoint** record containing *copies of the current Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table*, and updates the master record. Transactions and page flushes proceed concurrently — the tables captured are merely "fuzzy" snapshots, which is safe because analysis re-scans forward from begin_checkpoint and corrects them. Dirty pages are flushed *asynchronously* by background writers (PostgreSQL's checkpointer with `checkpoint_timeout`/`max_wal_size` and `checkpoint_completion_target` spreading writes; InnoDB's **adaptive flushing** driving fuzzy checkpoints based on redo-log fill ratio, with the **checkpoint LSN** = min recLSN effectively advancing as the flush list drains). The practical tradeoff: longer checkpoint intervals → less FPW/flush overhead but longer recovery (more redo).

  Note: PostgreSQL's recovery model is a simplification of ARIES — redo from the checkpoint's redo pointer repeating history, but **no undo pass** is needed for heap data because MVCC leaves dead/uncommitted tuples in place (visibility rules via CLOG/pg_xact make them invisible); vacuum reclaims them later. InnoDB, by contrast, performs genuine undo using its **undo logs** (stored in undo tablespaces, themselves redo-protected — "undo is logged").

### Mechanism 3: Shadow Paging (System R) — the Contrasting Approach

**Shadow paging** (Lorie, 1977; used in **System R** for intra-transaction/file recovery alongside logging) achieves atomicity *without* in-place updates:

- The database is accessed through a **page table** (page map) mapping logical page numbers to physical disk pages. At transaction/savepoint start, the current page table is the **shadow copy**, left untouched on disk.
- Every page update is **copy-on-write**: the page is written to a *new* physical location and the *current* (working) page table is updated to point to it; the shadow version still points to the old page.
- **Commit** is a single atomic act: atomically overwrite the root pointer so the current page table becomes the new shadow (one atomic sector write). **Abort/crash recovery** is trivial and instantaneous: discard the current table and revert to the shadow — a **NO-UNDO/NO-REDO** recovery scheme.

Why it lost to WAL (critique articulated in the ARIES paper and by the System R team's retrospective):
1. **Destroyed physical clustering/locality:** copy-on-write scatters logically sequential pages across disk, degrading scan performance.
2. **Garbage collection** of superseded pages and page-table maintenance overhead.
3. **Commit cost scales with page-table size** (flushing the updated map), and the indirection adds a lookup on every page access.
4. **Poor concurrency:** page-level granularity makes fine-grained (record-level) concurrent recovery and partial rollbacks awkward — System R still needed a log for multi-transaction concurrency and transaction-level undo.

Shadow-paging's ideas persist in modified forms: **LMDB** (copy-on-write B-tree with two root metapages — a true shadow-paging design, needing no WAL), **SQLite's rollback journal** mode (conceptually "before-image" rather than shadow, while SQLite's WAL mode is log-based), and copy-on-write filesystems (ZFS, Btrfs).

---

## Summary Table

| Concern | Mechanism | Key terms |
|---|---|---|
| WAL core | ARIES physiological logging | LSN, pageLSN, prevLSN, recLSN, DPT, TT, CLR, undoNextLSN, steal/no-force |
| Commit throughput | Group commit / log buffer flushing | force-log-at-commit, leader/follower flush, fsync batching, async commit |
| Torn pages | Full-page writes; doublewrite buffer | FPI after checkpoint (PostgreSQL); checksum-verified doublewrite area (InnoDB) |
| Recovery algorithm | ARIES three-phase restart | analysis → redo (repeating history) → undo with CLRs; restart idempotence |
| Bounding recovery | Fuzzy vs. sharp checkpoints | begin/end_checkpoint, master record, adaptive flushing, checkpoint LSN |
| Alternative design | Shadow paging (System R) | page table/shadow copy, copy-on-write, atomic root switch, NO-UNDO/NO-REDO |

response.content:
# MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

## Mechanism 1: PostgreSQL Tuple Versioning (xmin/xmax, Snapshots, VACUUM)

**Tuple-level versioning in heap.** PostgreSQL stores versions *in-place* in the heap table itself (no separate undo). Every tuple header carries system columns:

- **`xmin`**: the transaction ID (XID) of the inserting transaction.
- **`xmax`**: the XID of the deleting/updating transaction (0/invalid if live).
- **`ctid`**: the tuple's physical location; on UPDATE, the old version's `ctid` is redirected to point at the new version, forming an **update chain** (optimized by **HOT — Heap-Only Tuples** — when no indexed column changes and the new version fits on the same page, avoiding new index entries).
- **`cmin`/`cmax`**: command IDs for intra-transaction visibility (statements must not see their own in-progress changes incorrectly).

An UPDATE is implemented as delete + insert: set `xmax` on the old version, insert a new version with fresh `xmin`.

**Snapshots.** A snapshot captures: `xmin` (oldest XID still running — all XIDs below are decided), `xmax` (first unassigned XID — all at/above are invisible), and the list of in-progress XIDs (`xip`). A tuple is visible iff its inserting transaction committed before the snapshot and it is not deleted by a transaction that committed before the snapshot. Commit status is resolved via the **commit log (pg_xact/clog)**, cached in per-tuple **hint bits** (`HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, etc.). READ COMMITTED takes a snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE take one per transaction.

**VACUUM and wraparound.** Dead versions accumulate in the heap, so **VACUUM** reclaims tuples invisible to all snapshots (bounded by the oldest active snapshot / `xmin` horizon; long-running transactions and abandoned replication slots cause bloat). VACUUM also performs **freezing** (replacing old `xmin` with `FrozenTransactionId` / setting the frozen bit) to prevent **XID wraparound** on the 32-bit circular XID space, and maintains the **visibility map** (all-visible/all-frozen bits enabling index-only scans and vacuum skipping). **Autovacuum** triggers this based on dead-tuple thresholds.

## Mechanism 2: Undo-Log–Based MVCC — Oracle Rollback/Undo Segments and InnoDB Read Views

**Store-latest, reconstruct-old.** In contrast to PostgreSQL's append-new-version approach, Oracle and MySQL/InnoDB keep only the **newest version in place** and record before-images in **undo segments** (Oracle: rollback/undo segments in the undo tablespace; InnoDB: undo logs in rollback segments).

**Oracle.** Each data block header has an **Interested Transaction List (ITL)**. A reader compares the block/row's transaction info against its statement or transaction **SCN (System Change Number)**; if the version is too new, it follows the undo chain to construct a **Consistent Read (CR) block** — a reconstructed past image. If undo has been overwritten (undo_retention exceeded), the reader gets **ORA-01555 "snapshot too old."** Oracle's default READ COMMITTED gives statement-level consistency; SERIALIZABLE gives transaction-level Snapshot Isolation (it is SI, not true serializability — reported as ORA-08177 on write-write conflict).

**InnoDB.** Each clustered-index record carries hidden columns **`DB_TRX_ID`** (last modifier) and **`DB_ROLL_PTR`** (roll pointer into the undo log). Reads open a **read view** containing the set of active transaction IDs (`m_ids`), low/high watermarks (`up_limit_id`, `low_limit_id`); a record version is visible if its `DB_TRX_ID` is committed relative to the view, otherwise the reader walks the roll-pointer chain through undo records to rebuild the visible version. REPEATABLE READ uses one read view per transaction; READ COMMITTED one per statement. The **purge** threads garbage-collect undo records no longer needed by any read view (analogous to VACUUM, but rollback is cheap and old versions never bloat the main table — the trade-off is slower rollback-heavy workloads vs. PostgreSQL's cheap abort/expensive cleanup). Note: InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ also uses next-key locking for *locking reads* and writes (see B+tree section), which is why its RR is stronger than pure SI for some operations but still permits write skew for plain reads.

## Mechanism 3: Snapshot Isolation Anomalies and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

**Snapshot Isolation (SI).** Each transaction reads from a start-time snapshot; writes conflict under **First-Committer-Wins** (or first-updater-wins with locks): two concurrent transactions writing the same item cannot both commit. SI prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and (in most implementations) phantoms *in reads*, but is **not serializable**.

**Write skew.** The canonical SI anomaly: T1 reads {x, y}, writes x; T2 reads {x, y}, writes y; disjoint write sets → no ww-conflict → both commit, but the result corresponds to no serial order (e.g., two doctors both going off-call when the constraint requires ≥1 on-call). A related anomaly is the **read-only transaction anomaly** (Fekete et al. 2004), where even a read-only transaction can observe a non-serializable state. Also **phantom-based write skew**: predicate reads plus inserts that neither transaction's snapshot sees.

**Theory: rw-antidependencies and dangerous structures.** Model the Multi-version Serialization Graph: a **rw-antidependency** (rw-conflict) edge T1 →rw T2 exists when T1 reads a version and T2 writes a successor version of that item (T1 "reads under" T2's write). Adya/Fekete et al. proved every non-serializable SI execution contains a **dangerous structure**: two *consecutive* rw-antidependency edges T1 →rw T2 →rw T3 on a cycle, where T3 (the "pivot's" successor) commits first.

**SSI (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; PostgreSQL ≥ 9.1 SERIALIZABLE).** Run SI, but track rw-antidependencies with non-blocking **SIREAD locks** (predicate/page/tuple granularity in PostgreSQL, promotable under memory pressure, retained past commit until overlapping transactions finish). Each transaction tracks incoming/outgoing rw-conflict flags; when a transaction would become the **pivot** of a dangerous structure (both an inbound and outbound rw-antidependency among concurrent transactions), one participant is aborted with a **serialization failure** (SQLSTATE 40001), requiring retry. This is conservative (false positives — not every dangerous structure completes a cycle) but sound, giving true serializability without the blocking of two-phase locking. PostgreSQL adds the **safe snapshot** optimization for read-only transactions (`SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` waits for a snapshot provably free of anomalies, then needs no SIREAD tracking).

---

# B+Tree Maintenance

## Mechanism 1: Node Splits, Merges, and Rebalancing

**Splits.** Insertion into a full leaf of fanout-order *n* splits it: keys are divided (typically 50/50; many systems split rightmost-leaf insertions ~90/10 to optimize monotonic key loads), and a **separator key** is posted into the parent. If the parent is full, the split **propagates** upward; splitting the root grows tree height by one — the only way height increases, which keeps the tree perfectly height-balanced. Alternative to immediate split: **top-down preemptive splitting** (split any full node on the way down so a child split never propagates up — enables one-pass latch protocols).

**Deletes: merges and redistribution.** When deletion drops a node below minimum occupancy (classically ⌈n/2⌉), either **redistribute (rotate/borrow)** keys from a sibling and update the parent separator, or **merge (coalesce)** with a sibling, deleting the separator from the parent — which can cascade upward; collapsing the root's last child shrinks height. In practice, most production systems (and as analyzed by Johnson & Shasha, "free-at-empty") **do not eagerly rebalance on delete**: they let pages drain and reclaim them only when empty (e.g., PostgreSQL nbtree deletes empty pages via VACUUM; InnoDB merges only below `MERGE_THRESHOLD`), since eager merging thrashes under mixed workloads. Note B+tree specifics: all keys live in leaves, interior nodes hold only separators (which need not correspond to live keys), and leaves are chained with **sibling pointers** for range scans.

## Mechanism 2: Latch Crabbing / Lock Coupling and B-link Trees (Lehman–Yao)

**Latch crabbing (lock coupling).** Physical consistency of pages is protected by **latches** (short-term, non-transactional locks), distinct from transactional locks. Basic protocol: acquire child latch *before* releasing parent latch ("crab" down the tree). Readers couple shared latches. Writers pessimistically take exclusive latches but may release all ancestor latches once reaching a **safe node** (one that cannot split on insert / cannot underflow on delete). **Optimistic descent** improves concurrency: take shared latches down to the leaf, exclusive only on the leaf; if the leaf turns out unsafe (split needed), restart with the pessimistic protocol. Modern refinements: **optimistic lock coupling** using version counters (validate parent's version instead of holding its latch, restart on mismatch), as in ART/modern in-memory trees.

**B-link trees (Lehman & Yao 1981).** Eliminate latch coupling almost entirely by adding to every node (at every level) a **right-sibling pointer** and a **high key** (upper bound on keys reachable in/under that node). A split is decomposed into two atomic steps: (1) create the new right sibling, move the upper half of entries, set old node's high key and link pointer — a *half-split*; (2) later, post the separator into the parent. Between steps the tree is temporarily "inconsistent" but *correct*: any reader arriving at a node whose high key is less than its search key simply **moves right** along the link pointer until the key range covers the target. Consequently readers need **no latch coupling** (at most one latch at a time), and writers latch only the node being modified (plus the parent during separator posting, taken left-to-right/bottom-up to avoid deadlock). PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman–Yao B-link tree (with Lanin & Shasha-style additions for deletion/page reclamation and a left-link for backward scans).

## Mechanism 3: Structure Modification Operations (SMOs) and Key-Range / Next-Key Locking (ARIES/KVL, ARIES/IM)

**SMOs.** In the ARIES family (Mohan et al.), a split/merge/page-delete is a **Structure Modification Operation**: a multi-page atomic change that must appear atomic to concurrent transactions and be independently redoable/undoable despite the enclosing transaction possibly rolling back. ARIES/IM serializes SMOs with a **tree latch** (X for SMOs, acquired only when needed) and marks in-flight state with an **SM bit** on affected pages; SMOs are logged and made logically atomic via **nested top actions** — bracketed by a **dummy CLR (compensation log record)** whose UndoNxtLSN skips over the SMO's log records, so the SMO survives (is not undone) even if the initiating transaction aborts. In B-link designs, the half-split serves an analogous role: each atomic step leaves the tree search-correct.

**Key-range / next-key locking.** Transactional (logical) locking on index entries to achieve serializability and prevent **phantoms** without predicate locks. A key-range lock on key *k* covers the open interval from the previous key up to *k* (previous-key variants exist). Core protocols:

- **ARIES/KVL (Key-Value Locking, Mohan 1990):** locks on key values in the index; an insert/delete of key *k* also locks the **next key** (successor) to block phantom insertions into the gap; designed per-index, with IX/instant-duration optimizations for inserts into existing duplicate lists.
- **ARIES/IM (Index Management, Mohan & Levine 1992):** **data-only locking** — locks are on record IDs in the underlying table rather than per-index key values, so one lock covers the record across all indexes; still uses next-key locking on the index for phantom prevention, combined with the latch/SMO protocol above. Uses **instant-duration** locks where possible and commit-duration next-key locks on delete.
- **InnoDB next-key locks:** a row lock plus a **gap lock** on the interval preceding the index record (next-key lock = record lock + preceding gap lock); at REPEATABLE READ these prevent phantom inserts into scanned ranges; **insert intention locks** let non-conflicting inserts into the same gap proceed concurrently.

Graefe's later synthesis ("A Survey of B-tree Locking Techniques") formalizes the crucial separation this all rests on: **latches protect physical structure** (pages, held for the duration of a page operation, deadlock-avoided by ordering), while **locks protect logical content** (keys/ranges, held to commit under 2PL, deadlock-detected), and SMOs may commit independently of the transactions that triggered them.

# Findings: LSM Trees and Two-Phase Commit

## Part 1: Log-Structured Merge (LSM) Trees

### 1.1 Write Path: Memtable → SSTable Flush Pipeline

**Write-ahead log (WAL) + memtable.** Every write is first appended to a sequential WAL for durability, then inserted into the **memtable**, an in-memory sorted structure (typically a skip list in RocksDB/LevelDB, or a concurrent skip list / trie variant elsewhere). Writes are therefore sequential-I/O-bound and fast; updates and deletes are handled as new versions and **tombstones** rather than in-place mutation (the defining "log-structured" property).

**Immutable memtable and flush.** When the memtable reaches a size threshold (e.g., `write_buffer_size` in RocksDB), it is atomically swapped for a fresh memtable and marked **immutable**. A background flush thread serializes the immutable memtable into an **SSTable (Sorted String Table)**: an immutable, sorted-by-key file composed of data blocks, an index block (block index), filter block, and footer. After a successful flush, the corresponding WAL segment can be truncated/recycled.

**Write stalls and backpressure.** If flushes or compactions cannot keep up (too many immutable memtables, too many L0 files, or pending compaction bytes exceeding thresholds), the engine applies **write stalls/stops** — a key operational failure mode of LSM engines.

### 1.2 Compaction: Leveled vs. Size-Tiered

Compaction merges SSTables to bound read amplification and reclaim space from overwritten/deleted keys (dropping tombstones once they are older than all data they could shadow — Cassandra gates this with `gc_grace_seconds` to avoid resurrecting deleted data on replicas).

**Leveled compaction (RocksDB/LevelDB LCS).**
- Levels L1…Ln have exponentially increasing size targets (default fanout T ≈ 10). Within each level ≥ L1, SSTables are **non-overlapping in key range** (the level is a sorted run partitioned into files). L0 is special: files are whole flushed memtables and may overlap.
- Compaction picks a file in Li and merges it with the overlapping files in Li+1, rewriting into Li+1.
- **Trade-off:** low **read amplification** (at most one file per level must be consulted, ~O(log_T N) sorted runs) and low **space amplification** (~1.11× steady state, since ~90% of data is in the last level with duplicates mostly removed), but high **write amplification** — each key is rewritten up to T times per level, so total WA ≈ T × number-of-levels (often 10–30×).

**Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra STCS; RocksDB "universal" is a close relative).**
- SSTables of similar size are grouped into **tiers**; when a tier accumulates `min_threshold` (default 4) similar-sized tables, they are merged into one larger table in the next tier.
- **Trade-off:** low write amplification (each key rewritten ~once per tier, WA ≈ O(log_T N)) and high flush/ingest throughput, but higher **read amplification** (multiple overlapping sorted runs per tier must all be checked) and worst-case **space amplification up to ~2× or more** (a full-tier merge temporarily needs space for inputs + output; overlapping runs retain stale versions longer).
- Cassandra also offers **LCS** (leveled, for read-heavy/update-heavy workloads) and **TWCS (Time-Window Compaction Strategy)** for time-series data, which compacts only within time windows and drops whole expired SSTables via TTL.

**Lazy-leveling / hybrids.** Systems like the **Dostoevsky/LSM-bush** line of work (Dayan & Idreos) formalize the leveling-vs-tiering continuum: tier the smaller levels, level only the largest, tuning the merge policy per level to the workload.

### 1.3 Read Path Optimizations

A point read must consult memtable(s), then SSTables from newest to oldest. Named mechanisms:

1. **Bloom filters.** Each SSTable (or each data block, or per-level in RocksDB prefix/full filters) carries a Bloom filter over its keys. A negative lookup skips the file entirely without I/O; false-positive rate is tunable via bits/key (~10 bits/key ⇒ ~1% FPR). Variants: blocked Bloom filters, **ribbon filters** (RocksDB), and Cassandra's per-SSTable filters. **Monkey** (Dayan et al.) shows optimal filter-memory allocation skews bits toward smaller levels. Note: Bloom filters do not help **range scans**, which must merge-iterate every overlapping run (prefix Bloom filters and SuRF-style tries partially address this).

2. **Fence pointers / block indexes.** Each SSTable has a sparse **index block** holding the first (or a divider) key of every data block ("fence pointers"), enabling a binary search to identify the single candidate block, so a positive lookup costs ~1 data-block read. Two-level/partitioned indexes (RocksDB partitioned index/filter) keep index memory bounded for huge files. Additional metadata: per-file min/max keys (used for level-file pruning), and Cassandra's partition index + key cache.

3. **Block cache and row cache.** Uncompressed/compressed block caches (RocksDB LRU/Clock cache) absorb hot reads; OS page cache sits beneath.

4. **Merge iterators with heap-based k-way merge** for range scans across runs, plus **seek-based tombstone skipping** and range tombstones (RocksDB `DeleteRange`) to avoid scanning dead data.

### 1.4 RUM Conjecture Framing

The **RUM conjecture** (Athanassoulis et al., 2016): an access method cannot be simultaneously optimal in **Read amplification, Update (write) amplification, and Memory/space amplification**; optimizing two degrades the third. LSM tuning is a direct instance:
- **Leveling:** minimizes R and M, pays in U (high write amplification).
- **Tiering:** minimizes U, pays in R (more runs to probe) and M (stale versions, transient merge space).
- **Bloom filters/fence pointers:** buy back R by spending M (memory for filters/indexes).
This continuum is explicitly navigated by tunables (fanout T, tiering threshold K, bits-per-key) and by hybrid designs (lazy leveling, universal compaction).

## Part 2: Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

### 2.1 Core Protocol

Participants: one **coordinator (transaction manager)** and N **participants (resource managers/cohorts)**. All sites use write-ahead logging with **force-write** (flush before replying) at the critical points.

**Phase 1 — voting/prepare phase.**
1. Coordinator sends **PREPARE** to all participants.
2. Each participant that can commit force-writes a **prepared** log record (redo+undo info durable), enters the **prepared/in-doubt state**, and replies **VOTE-COMMIT (YES)**. It thereby surrenders its unilateral abort right and must hold locks. Otherwise it replies **VOTE-ABORT (NO)** and may abort immediately.

**Phase 2 — decision/commit phase.**
3. If all votes are YES, the coordinator force-writes a **commit record** (the commit point) and sends **COMMIT**; on any NO or timeout it logs/decides **ABORT** and sends ABORT.
4. Participants apply the decision, write their own commit/abort record, release locks, and send **ACK**. After all ACKs, the coordinator writes an **end/forget** record and discards transaction state.

**Guarantee:** atomic commitment — AC1–AC5 (all participants reach the same decision; commit only if all voted yes; decision is irreversible; termination under eventual repair).

### 2.2 Presumed-Abort and Presumed-Commit Optimizations

These reduce log force-writes and messages for the recovery/inquiry path (Mohan, Lindsay & Obermarck, 1986; presumed-abort is the industry default, e.g., in the XA / DTC ecosystem).

**Presumed abort (PA).**
- Convention: if the coordinator has **no information** about a transaction (after inquiry), the answer is **ABORT**.
- Consequences: the coordinator need **not force** the abort record, needs **no ACKs for aborts**, and participants need not force abort records; **read-only participants** reply VOTE-READ-ONLY and are excluded from phase 2 entirely (the read-only optimization). Cost is unchanged on the commit path (commit record still forced, commit ACKs still needed so the coordinator knows when to forget).

**Presumed commit (PC).**
- Convention: absence of information means **COMMIT**. Removes the need for commit ACKs and for participants to force commit records.
- But to make abort safe, the coordinator must **force-write a collecting/initiation record before sending PREPARE** (recording the participant set), so that after a crash it knows which in-doubt transactions it had started and must presume nothing incorrectly. Net: PC favors workloads where nearly all transactions commit; PA is cheaper for aborts and read-only work, which is why PA won in practice. ("New presumed commit" variants reduce PC's extra force.)

### 2.3 The Blocking Problem and Coordinator Failure (In-Doubt Transactions)

- A participant that has voted YES is **in-doubt (prepared)**: it cannot unilaterally commit (another participant may have voted NO) or abort (the coordinator may have logged commit). If the **coordinator fails** (or is partitioned away) at this point, the participant **blocks**, holding locks and prepared-state resources until the coordinator recovers or a resolution protocol answers its inquiry — this is 2PC's defining weakness as a **blocking atomic commitment protocol**.
- **Cooperative termination protocol:** an in-doubt participant queries other participants; if any has received COMMIT/ABORT, or any has not yet voted (so abort is safe), the transaction resolves. But if **all surviving participants are in-doubt**, blocking persists.
- Theory: a **window of vulnerability** is unavoidable for any atomic commit protocol under communication failure; non-blocking ACP is impossible with network partitions (Skeen & Stonebraker), and the FLP impossibility result bounds asynchronous solutions generally. Operationally this surfaces as **heuristic decisions** (XA heuristic commit/abort), which can violate atomicity and require manual reconciliation.

### 2.4 Enhancements

**1. Three-phase commit (3PC) — Skeen, 1981.**
- Inserts a **pre-commit (prepared-to-commit)** phase between voting and commit: coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT after unanimous YES; only after all acknowledge pre-commit does it send COMMIT. The invariant: no participant commits while another could still be in a state from which abort is possible — removing the state where survivors can't tell the decision apart.
- **Non-blocking under crash-stop failures with a synchronous network** (via an elected new coordinator running a termination protocol), but **not safe under network partitions** (two partitions can decide differently) and costs an extra round trip. Hence rarely deployed; it's mainly of pedagogical/historical importance. (Quorum-based 3PC variants, e.g., Keidar & Dolev's E3PC, address partitions but converge toward consensus.)

**2. Paxos Commit — Gray & Lamport, 2006.**
- Reframes atomic commit as consensus: **each participant's vote (prepared/aborted) is decided by its own Paxos instance** replicated across 2F+1 acceptors; the transaction commits iff every instance chooses "prepared."
- The coordinator role is stateless/replaceable (any node can act as leader of the Paxos instances), so **coordinator failure no longer blocks**: the protocol tolerates F faults non-blockingly. With F=0 it degenerates to ordinary 2PC (showing 2PC is the F=0 special case). Message complexity is higher but the fault-tolerance delay is the same two message delays on the fast path (using the Paxos "phase 1 pre-execution" optimization).

**3. Consensus-replicated coordinator/participant state — Spanner's 2PC over Paxos groups (Corbett et al., 2012).**
- Data is sharded into **Paxos groups** (each group a Multi-Paxos replicated state machine). For a multi-group transaction, the **Paxos leader of one group acts as 2PC coordinator**; leaders of other groups are participants.
- Every critical 2PC log record — each participant's **prepare record** and the coordinator's **commit record** — is **replicated through Paxos** within its group before being acted on. Thus "coordinator failure" means only a leader failover: a new leader reads the replicated log and completes the protocol. 2PC's blocking window is eliminated as long as a majority of each group survives: the unreliable single-node coordinator is replaced by a highly available replicated one.
- Spanner layers two-phase locking and **TrueTime**-based commit timestamps on top (commit-wait for external consistency), but the atomic-commit core is exactly 2PC with consensus-durable state. The same pattern appears in CockroachDB (transaction record in a Raft-replicated range, plus the **parallel commits** optimization that makes the commit point an implicit quorum condition reducing commit latency to ~1 round of consensus), TiDB (Percolator-style 2PC over Raft), and FoundationDB.

**Supplementary named optimizations:** **read-only optimization** (one-phase for read-only participants, subsumed by PA), **transfer-of-commit / last-agent optimization** (coordinator delegates the decision to the last participant, saving a message round), **one-phase commit (1PC)** when only a single participant did writes, and **early prepare / unsolicited vote** (piggybacking prepare on the final work message).

### 2.5 Summary Table

| Mechanism | Coordinator-failure behavior | Extra cost | Partition-safe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain 2PC (presumed abort) | Participants block in-doubt | Baseline | Safe but blocking |
| Presumed commit | Same blocking | Extra forced collecting record; fewer commit ACKs | Same |
| 3PC | Non-blocking (crash-stop, synchronous) | +1 round trip | **No** (can split-brain) |
| Paxos Commit | Non-blocking with ≤F acceptor faults | ~2F more messages per participant | Yes |
| Spanner-style 2PC over Paxos/Raft groups | Leader failover completes protocol | Consensus latency per log record | Yes (majority per group) |
